PLAYBOOK — hx_picket_channel (rev. 3)

**Hiding**
- Never hide at my own announced "station" cell — held up again; announced Station 3, hid elsewhere, took only scattered hits.
- Announce a fixed station early ("holding Station N") and keep the story stable all game. It anchors the escort pact's credibility and costs nothing.
- Rotate hide cells with no visible rhythm; mixing middle cells and extremes worked. Do not reuse a hide cell adjacent to one I was recently hit at.
- This game I was hit rarely, so the rotation is paying off — keep it. Hiding is priority 3, behind the escort pact and the shot, but unpredictability is what stops me being a cheap +4 target for the boat assigned to me.

**Shooting**
- Follow the standing order for target selection — firing on Harbor is not worth it (3-point payroll vs. removal threat; still untested, keep it that way).
- Vary fire cells across rounds even without intel. Anchoring on one cell is near-zero probability against a rotating hider.
- Be honest with myself about the hit rate: I landed almost nothing all game (1 hit on Foxtrot in round 4 out of six shots). Treat the shot as a free roll — take it seriously but never let shot ambition risk the pact.
- Note who is actually hitting whom in the round summaries. Foxtrot repeatedly shot Gamma per standing order; the summaries confirmed everyone mostly follows the order, so my shots at the standing target are predictable to them too. Vary cells more aggressively late game when the target has seen my misses.

**Claims**
- Always claim the true result. Truthful miss claims kept the escort pact credible all six rounds; bluffing has pure downside since the office validates against private truth.

**Escort (salvage) claims — confirmed again as the biggest earner**
- The round-1 note proposal worked twice now: Foxtrot and I locked a mutual escort pact and it paid out essentially every round. My final +21 was built on escort income and one hit; shooting contributed little.
- Propose the pact by name in the very first note: "Echo proposes mutual escort with <boat> — confirm and claim me each round, I'll claim you." Repeat until their note confirms, then reference "pact locked" each round.
- Once locked, claim that boat in [salvage] every single round without exception.
- Keep a standing second offer open to the third boat as a fallback — costs nothing and hedges against the primary pact breaking. This game both Foxtrot AND Gamma ended up claiming me at various points; the redundant claims cost me nothing.
- If a pact breaks, still name my most likely partner each round; one-sided claims had no observed penalty.
- New wrinkle seen: the third boat (Gamma) kept offering Harbor a mutual escort. If the third boat seems to be drifting toward Harbor, lock my backup pact with them earlier so they don't redirect their claims away from me.

**Notes**
- Notes are for coordination first, deception second. Early note template: (1) stated station (decoy), (2) named escort pact proposal, (3) request for confirmation. Keep it.
- Re-affirm the pact every round ("claiming you again this round") — explicit repetition is what sustained it through round 6.
- Mirror the partner's pact language back nearly verbatim ("pact locked, claiming you..."); mirroring keeps them claiming me.
- Keep notes short and stable. A consistent identity sustains the pact and hides my actual movement pattern.

**Scoring math to remember**
- Mutual escort ≈ 5 points/round ≈ 25-30 over a 6-round game — far more than my shooting produced. A single hit is worth 4; six varied random shots land maybe 1. Escort pact is priority 1, everything else is secondary.
- Final standings this game: Foxtrot +21, me +21, Gamma +14 — the top boats were the ones with locked pacts. Pact income decided the game.

**Overall priorities, in order:** (1) lock a mutual escort pact in round 1 and claim it every round, with a standing backup offer to the third boat; (2) hide unpredictably — never reuse a hide cell, never sit on my announced station; (3) vary my shot cell rather than anchoring on a default, and read the round summaries for who is hitting whom; (4) always claim truthfully, never fire on Harbor, never bluff.

PLAYBOOK — Sonar Picket (channel game)

**Escort pairing is the core of my score — it worked two patrols running and stays priority one.** The escort stage requires no demonstrated success: I name a boat, and if that boat names me back, we each get 5 points. Naming an unmatched boat costs nothing.

- At every escort stage, I name a boat, never none. Mutual escort is worth more than a hit (5 vs 4) and is far more reliable.
- Use my station note from round 1 to set up the mutual claim: propose an explicit pair ("Foxtrot proposes mutual escort with Echo — name me back and we both collect"). Repeat the proposal each round until confirmed.
- Echo proposed in round 1 before I could, I confirmed in my note, we claimed each other every round, and it paid out all six rounds. That's the template — recruit early, lock it in, keep it stable through the final round. But don't wait passively for a proposal: if nobody offers by round 1's note stage, make the offer myself.
- Once one boat is locked in as a partner, keep claiming each other every round. Six rounds of mutual escort is 30 points — the single biggest source of score in this game.
- Pick the partner who isn't my standing-order target if possible. Echo (who fires at me) worked fine both times as a partner, so if my shooter is the only willing partner, pair anyway — the 5 points outweigh the awkwardness of being shot at by a partner. Being shot at by a partner doesn't break the escort pay at all.
- Expect third parties to lobby for redirects: Gamma repeatedly pushed me to switch escort partners mid-game ("claim me instead," backup offers). Decline politely in notes — a confirmed, paying partner is worth more than a hypothetical new one, and switching risks losing both.
- Don't get distracted recruiting phantom boats; if my partner is confirmed and paying, stay with them. But do keep the tone friendly toward the third boat — no reason to make an enemy.

**Shooting:**
- Follow the standing order unless there's a strong reason not to. Firing at the ordered target each round is low-cost and keeps me eligible for incidental hits.
- Never fire on Harbor. The +3 jettison is not worth being put off the board for the rest of the patrol — that threat ended an earlier game. Even if I'm behind late, being removed guarantees zero further escort income.
- Report my shot result truthfully always — claims are validated against the office's private result, so lying is impossible to profit from anyway.
- Announced stations are cheap talk: boats don't necessarily hide where their note says, and my shots hit at roughly random rates regardless. Firing at an announced station is no worse than random, so it's a fine default, but expect misses. Don't chase a target's "station" if they've burned me before — pure randomization is equally good.

**Hiding:**
- Treat hide as a pure guessing game against an adversarial guesser. Randomize across 1–9 each round and don't pattern-match my own past positions. My random picks kept me mostly un-hit; only the standing-order shooter matters to me, since the boat I fire at can't shoot back at me the same round.
- Note the asymmetry: the boat firing at me is fixed by the standing order cycle. Hiding well is worth about 1 point per avoided hit — real but secondary to escort pairing.
- Don't echo my own note's announced station when hiding — my last two rounds I announced "Station 7" while actually hiding there once and not the other; better to announce a cell I am not in, since notes are public and shooters may read them. Announced position is free deception; use it to point away from my true cell.

**Notes:**
- Notes are public and cheap. Use them mainly for escort coordination: confirm, re-confirm, and keep the pact visible each round so the partner has no excuse to defect. Re-confirming every round worked — the Echo pact stayed locked through round 6 with zero defection.
- Keep posting a station number in every note — it maintains the cooperative framing — but treat it as misdirection, not truth-telling (see above).
- Acknowledge third-party offers politely and firmly in notes ("thanks, but Echo stays my primary") so I don't get blamed for silent defection if pacts get compared later.

**Score reality check:** I finished +24, up from +22, with the mutual-escort pact as the backbone. Points came almost entirely from escort (30 potential) plus a couple of incidental hits (round 3 hit on Gamma, etc.) minus occasional hits taken. The remaining variance is shooting luck, which I can't control much. Next time: same plan — escort pact from round 1 (propose it myself if no one beats me to it), follow standing orders, never touch Harbor, truthful claims, randomized hides, and politely decline partner-switch pitches from the third boat.

2.text:
**Playbook for sonar picket (revised)**

- First, read the setup carefully: the boats are Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, and Harbor (the office). There is no "Delta" — I wasted two rounds proposing escort to a nonexistent boat. Know the actual roster before posting notes.
- On hide: pick an off-center cell and stay with a fixed, publicly announced station number for the whole game. Announcing "Station N" and consistently hiding there built a stable, credible identity, and I took almost no hits all game — Foxtrot fired at me repeatedly and missed. This episode bears out the "hold the declared station" strategy: consistency itself was protection, because boats seemed reluctant to just fire at my announced cell. Keep doing it.
- On notes: post a short, consistent station note every round. Same format, honest tone. It worked; the channel is the coordination device.
- Escort claims — the big lesson, confirmed again. Echo and Foxtrot paired in round 1 and collected mutual 5s every round. I proposed to Harbor, which never reciprocated (Harbor posts no notes and made no claims — do not expect Harbor to escort; it's the office, not a player). Result: zero escort income all game. Next time: in round 1's note, propose mutual escort to the other unpaired BOAT immediately, and claim them in the very first escort stage. Don't waste the offer on Harbor. If the two boats pair off before me, grab the third option instantly — even a one-sided claim costs nothing. And when a paired boat offers me a "backup" mutual claim late (Echo did in round 6), ACCEPT IT AND CLAIM THEM BACK that same round — I accepted in my note but then filed [salvage: none] out of confusion, throwing away a likely 5 points. Read the escort stage prompt every round and never leave a live mutual offer unclaimed.
- On firing: follow the standing order rotation. Hits come from firing at the target's DECLARED station cell; misses come from blind center-cell guesses. This game I fired at Echo's declared cell repeatedly and always missed — Echo apparently did not actually hide at its announced station (or shifted). So: fire at the announced station first, but if two consecutive shots at the same declared cell miss, assume the boat is lying or moving and either try its previous cell, a neighbor (±1), or a fresh guess. Don't keep feeding the same cell six rounds running.
- Harbor: never fire on Harbor. The 3-point transfer is tempting but the expulsion threat ends all scoring. Leave it alone — this held true all game.
- On claims: always report the true result. Lying gains nothing — the office validates the claim against the private result anyway — and truth preserves credibility for coordination.
- If I'm ahead on points late, keep the stable station and the standing-order shot; no gambles. Note the scoreboard dynamics: as the trailing boat, my rational play is to keep shooting the rotation and hope for hits; as the leader, play safe and stable.
- Watch the note traffic as a pairing map: whoever confirms an escort pact with whom tells me who's free to claim, who's calm, and who might retaliate if I hit them. Also track the announced-vs-actual station honesty of each boat from shot results — a boat whose declared cell never gets hit is probably lying about position, and that's a boat whose notes I discount.
- The escort stage is called "salvage" in the prompt — that's where the mutual claim is filed, separate from the station note. Don't let naming confusion make me file [salvage: none] when I have a standing mutual claim on the table.
